questions.q: In which year did Gandhi explicitly announce his focus on the Constructive Programme (khadi, Harijan, village reconstruction) after his release from prison?
questions.a: 1924. After his release in February 1924, Gandhi "chose to devote his attention to the promotion of home-spun cloth (khadi), and the abolition of untouchability" (NCERT, p. 294). A wrong answer (e.g., 1920 or 1930) reveals the student conflates the Constructive Programme with the Non-Cooperation Movement launch or the Salt March, missing that Gandhi deliberately paused mass civil disobedience after Chauri Chaura to build social infrastructure.

questions.q: Why did Gandhi choose the charkha (spinning wheel) as the central symbol of the Constructive Programme, rather than a purely political symbol like the flag?
questions.a: The charkha simultaneously addressed economic, social, and symbolic dimensions: (1) Economic — it provided supplementary income to the rural poor and reduced dependence on British mill-cloth; (2) Social — it erased the caste boundary between mental labour (traditionally upper-caste) and manual labour (traditionally lower-caste); (3) Symbolic — it represented a non-exploitative, human-scale technology against industrial capitalism. A wrong answer focusing only on "Swadeshi" or "boycott of foreign cloth" misses the caste-transcending and anti-industrial modernity dimensions Gandhi explicitly articulated in Young India (1924, 1927).

questions.q: During the 1930 Dandi March, Gandhi told upper-caste villagers at Wasna: "If you are out for Swaraj you must serve untouchables. You won't get Swaraj merely by the repeal of the salt taxes." Apply this statement to explain why Gandhi made Harijan uplift a non-negotiable condition for Swaraj, not just a parallel social service.
questions.a: Gandhi argued that Swaraj meant self-rule at every level — including the self's relationship to the most marginalised. Untouchability was not merely a "social evil" but a structural violence that corrupted the moral authority needed to demand justice from the British. By making Harijan service a precondition, Gandhi forced nationalists to confront internal hierarchy before claiming external sovereignty. A wrong answer treating Harijan work as "charity" or "reform" separate from politics misses Gandhi's core argument: political freedom without social equality reproduces domination in a new form.

questions.q: Compare the Constructive Programme's approach to village reconstruction with the British colonial model of rural development. Identify two fundamental differences in their assumptions about village autonomy and economic logic.
questions.a: Difference 1: Autonomy — Gandhi's village reconstruction (Gram Swaraj) envisioned self-governing, self-sufficient village republics controlling their own resources and disputes; the British model (e.g., through District Collectors and revenue systems) centralised authority and extracted surplus. Difference 2: Economic logic — Gandhi prioritised need-based, labour-intensive, local production (khadi, village industries) for local consumption; the British prioritised cash-crop cultivation for global markets and machine-made imports. A wrong answer listing only "Gandhi wanted villages to be clean" or "British built railways" misses the systemic contrast in governance philosophy and political economy.

questions.q: Evaluate the critique that Gandhi's Constructive Programme was "utopian" and "anti-modern" because it rejected industrial machinery and centralised planning. Use evidence from Gandhi's own writings (Young India, 1924, 1927) to defend or refute.
questions.a: Refutation with nuance: Gandhi did not reject all machinery — he wrote "Khaddar does not seek to destroy all machinery but it does regulate its use... The wheel is itself an exquisite piece of machinery" (Young India, 1927). His objection was to labour-displacing, capital-intensive machinery that concentrated wealth ("craze for machinery... thousands are without work"). He advocated appropriate technology serving the poorest. The "utopian" label ignores that khadi provided actual livelihood to millions during the 1930s Depression when industrial employment collapsed. A wrong answer either uncritically accepts the "anti-modern" label or claims Gandhi rejected all technology, missing his sophisticated critique of industrial capitalism's distributional consequences.

questions.q: Construct a historical argument: "The Constructive Programme was Gandhi's most radical contribution to Indian nationalism because it redefined the 'nation' not as a territorial-political unit but as a daily ethical practice." Support with three specific examples from the 1924-1935 period.
questions.a: Example 1: Khadi — wearing hand-spun cloth made nationalism a tactile, daily choice accessible to women, peasants, and the poor, not just lawyers petitioning the British. Example 2: Harijan service — upper-caste volunteers cleaning "untouchable" quarters and sharing meals transformed caste hierarchy from abstract principle to lived practice, making the "nation" inclusive in action. Example 3: Nai Talim (Basic Education) — integrating spinning, agriculture, and craft with literacy redefined education as preparation for productive citizenship, not clerical employment. A poor answer lists activities without showing how each redefined national belonging; a strong answer demonstrates the shift from "nation as sovereign territory" to "nation as community of ethical practice."

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Gandhi's Constructive Programme (1920s-1940s) was a comprehensive social reform agenda that ran parallel to political resistance, centred on khadi (hand-spun cloth) for economic self-reliance, Harijan uplift (abolition of ______), village reconstruction through sanitation and local governance, and Nai Talim (basic education) integrating manual labour with learning — all designed to build a morally and materially self-sufficient nation capable of true Swaraj.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you visit a village in Gujarat today and see a khadi bhandar, a school where children learn weaving alongside reading, and a community ______ drive — all tracing back to Gandhi's 1920s vision.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you visit a village in Gujarat today and see a khadi bhandar, a school where children learn weaving alongside reading, and a community sanitation drive — all tracing back to Gandhi's ______s vision.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can explain how each component of the Constructive Programme (khadi, Harijan work, village reconstruction, basic education) addressed specific structural weaknesses in Indian society, and can analyse why Gandhi insisted social reform was a prerequisite for political freedom, using evidence from his speeches and the 1930 Dandi.
